items.question: How do you think the development of AI-enabled tools should shape priorities for biological defense?
items.object: AI-enabled tools and the offense-defense balance in biosecurity
items.answer: What we're seeing at the minute is really rapid development of new capabilities through the development of AI enabled tools. The correlary of that is that there's a capability jump for malicious actors as well. If someone wants to cause harm using biology—and thank god not that many people do, which is great—but if someone were to want to do so, they now have more powerful tools available to them than they did 5 years ago. What we want to do is try to privilege defenders who are making counter measures against those who are seeking to cause harm.

items.question: Where do you think human responsibility should sit when AI is used to speed up processes leading to regulatory approval?
items.object: Human accountability in AI-assisted regulatory approval
items.answer: It's really important to think about the application of AI and the development and where should we pour money into it should be into speeding other pieces up and again never removing the human from that decision-making process. It still needs to be a human that makes the decision to whether or not something gets regulatory approval. All of that needs to have humans ultimately liable because there could be side effects down the line and there needs to be a degree of accountability that sits with people not with black boxes.

items.question: How do you think about shifting the offense-defense balance for AI-enabled biological tools?
items.object: The offense-defense balance for AI-enabled biological tools
items.answer:
What we're seeing at the minute is really rapid development of new capabilities through the development of AI-enabled tools, in particular narrow tools or AI scientific tools, but also obviously LLMs. Everyone will have noticed that between three years ago and now it's a completely different world. What you can do with these tools has materially changed. What a lot of people won't have seen is that the extent to which LLMs have shifted in their capability over that time has been mirrored to some extent in narrow tools that scientists will use to do novel, innovative science and come up with new medical countermeasures like vaccines and antibiotics and even diagnostics. So all of that is happening sort of below the surface, at a level that the average person on the street isn't noticing because they're not involved in cutting-edge frontier science. But there is that same capability jump.

The implication or the corollary of that is that there's a capability jump for malicious actors as well. So if someone wants to cause harm using biology—and thank God not that many people do, which is great—but if someone were to want to do so, they now have more powerful tools available to them than they did three, five years ago. So the offense-defense balance is sort of how much uplift, how much easier is it for good actors, the scientists that are making countermeasures? How much uplift are they receiving versus how much uplift malicious actors or people who want to cause harm are receiving from the same tools?

What we want to do is try to privilege defenders who are making those countermeasures against those who are seeking to cause harm. And there's a number of different ways that we can try to do that. But a lot of that is making the latest tools available to defenders before offenders. Project Glass Wing is kind of the cybersecurity equivalent of this, when Anthropic went out with this brand-new model and said, “Right, this is too powerful. We can't just release this willy-nilly. We have to make sure that we do it in a careful and structured way.” So they released it first to several financial institutions and banks so that they could go through their codebase and make sure that a lot of the bugs that have been identified by Mythos could be fixed prior to that being released in the public domain.

There's a similar need in the biological space, but there isn't as much of an awareness of that, or there isn't as clear a pathway for that to happen as there was with Mythos. I think that the implications of the harm that could happen are more theoretical in some people's minds than cybersecurity causing issues, causing massive losses of financial capital within banking institutions. So we're trying to promote this idea of shifting the offense-defense balance within AI-enabled tools, and it's finding some traction.

items.question: Why do you see equitable access to AI models and tools as a difficult part of prioritizing biological defenders?
items.object: Equitable access to AI models and tools when prioritizing biological defense
items.answer: We're trying to promote this idea of shifting the offense-defense balance within AI-enabled tools, and it's finding some traction, but obviously it's really difficult to do that in a way that's equitable. So we just put out a paper—my line manager Dr. Cassidy Nelson, one of our contractors, Sharon Milanza, have put out a paper on equitable access to AI models and AI-enabled tools—which I think is a really important dimension of this. Because while you're trying to privilege defensive actors, you might exclude some defensive actors who maybe don't have traditional signs of legitimacy that we would expect, like an institutional email address or a really long publication track record. And so trying to do this in a way that reduces risk but also is equitable is a really, really difficult challenge.

items.question: How do you think releasing increasingly powerful AI models without moderating public access would affect the risk of biological misuse?
items.object: Unmoderated public release of increasingly powerful AI models and biological misuse
items.answer: I guess again we can go back to sort of the mythos example of if they had just released it to the general public, what would have happened? And I think what would have happened is people would have mayhem through cyber attacks etc. And I think the same applies here. If we just release increasingly powerful models that have increasingly strong capabilities into the public domain and we do nothing to sort of moderate that, then I think that what you might see is people starting to use them to cause harm. And again, some of that though will derive fundamentally from the extent to which people want to use biology as a way to cause harm, which is a sort of whole different kettle of fish with interdicting, counterterroring, that whole world. But yeah, I think it's kind of inevitable to some extent if you put more powerful capabilities into people's hands that statistically some portion of people will want to cause harm, so they will use the capabilities available to them. So I think that's the risk.

items.question: Why do you see know-your-customer checks as a promising way to control access to powerful AI and biological capabilities?
items.object: Know-your-customer checks for access to powerful AI and biological capabilities
items.answer:
My take at the minute is that robust know your customer or KYC checks are sort of one of the most promising avenues for ensuring that the capabilities get delivered into the right hands. Ensuring that you know who is using it, what their purpose is and then assessing whether that purpose is legitimate. And so that's true for powerful AI models, that's true for nucleic acid synthesis. Basically, when it comes down to it, you want to know when you're putting capabilities out there, who's using it and why.

And that's quite difficult to check, but again, we've just put out a paper in the synthesis screening space looking at how using LLMs can increase the efficiency or reduce the cost, depending on how you want to look at it, of information retrieval and collation when you are trying to figure out whether a person is a real person and whether they have a legitimate purpose. But you could do the exact same thing for having access to an AI model, right? A frontier model or an AI scientific tool or whatever it is.

Currently, if we look at what's being done, you look at something like GPT Rosland. It's a sort of trusted partner program where OpenAI is only giving access to very select few people and increasing that by very few people per month. I think something like two extra groups per month are getting approved because it's a very slow laborious process that they have to do a lot of due diligence and verify that they are in fact really exclusively defensive actors and they're only going to do good with this, and so it's okay to give them access to the model that's been fine-tuned on biological data. That's incredibly slow and it's not a really viable solution in the long term for everyone. So like somewhere like OpenAI that has enormous amounts of resource can do something like that. It can take a month and people want access to it so bad that they'll wait. But you need a more structured way of doing that.

And so this is why we were looking at whether you can use LLMs to sort of try and gather that information and collect it. And then ultimately you still have a human that makes a decision as to whether or not a person should gain access to something. It's not human out of the loop system by any means. The decision-making and the liability still falls with the person. But at least the information gathering phase, instead of it being someone googling like is this person real, you can just have a series of APIs that get called by an LLM to gather that information as a structured way that then gets handed as a report to a human that makes the decision. So I think that is our best bet at the minute for controlling access to more dangerous capabilities.

items.question: How do you think managed access using LLM-assisted know-your-customer checks should account for the risk of excluding legitimate researchers and startups?
items.object: Equity and exclusion in managed access using LLM-assisted know-your-customer checks
items.answer:
There absolutely is a risk of that, and it's always really difficult when you're talking about managed access to balance those considerations. We, in the study specifically on using LLM for KYC checks in the context of synthetic nucleic acids, did try to generate a test data set of scientists from different jurisdictions and see whether there was a greater or lower success rate at retrieving that information on the basis of the information that was out there. Because the LLM is only as good as the information that it's able to gather and what's in its training data set. It's kind of the same old garbage in, garbage out problem. If you don't have good data, you can't produce a good output.

And we found that pretty regularly we had more refusals by the human judges based on the information provided to them by the LM for researchers, I think, based in China and in the global south. And part of that was driven by researchers in China using Gmail addresses rather than .edu or .ac.uk or whatever the top level domain is for your educational institutions. Because a lot of them use personal Gmail addresses, that was seen as like a red flag or whatever, and as a result there was more refusal ultimately because they didn't use that same thing.

So there is an issue with equity or elitism, because if all you're looking for is, oh, this person has an institutional email address, now they're legit, what do you do with stealth startups that are just starting out? Maybe it's some grad students who are operating out of a warehouse or a science park. They don't want people to know about the company yet. There might not be a registry in the UK with Company's House, or the equivalent, which shows that it's a registered company. How do you deal with those kinds of cases, and do you just accept that all of that innovation gets prevented? And the answer is obviously no. I think that there needs to be a smarter way of going about it. But at least we're having these conversations now, and at least we can try and iterate on these systems over time.

items.question: Why do you see supply chain and logistics tools as a promising area for defensive AI in biosecurity?
items.object: AI integration into medical countermeasure supply chains
items.answer:
I think that your classic answers are going to be protein language models and genome language models and improving those types of frontier AI biomodels. I think that that's a little bit narrow. Even though that's a very important conversation to have, there's actually a lot of opportunities for the integration of AI into things that we don't necessarily think of as being that first line. So I'm thinking specifically of supply chain and logistics tools which are used by government to visualize and understand flows of all sorts of materials, but also medical countermeasures.

I've done quite a lot of work on supply chain resilience for medical countermeasures in the UK, and there's a really great program, the global supply chain intelligence platform or program, which is owned by the department for business and trade, but which is now participated in by seven different government departments. It's a platform which tracks, I think, 600 million different types of items and their flows around the UK. It's a really promising platform for understanding global supply chains and how those flows affect the UK. To some extent they are using some machine learning and some data analytics, but I think there's a much bigger opportunity for integration of AI into those kinds of tools, not just in the UK but more widely across the world.

Being able to know where your countermeasures are, when they're going to get to you, when they expire once you have them, where they are in your country if you're stockpiling them—there's not that sort of integrated supply chain visibility across the United Kingdom yet, despite GIP being a very, very strong program. It doesn't include the Department of Transport data yet. So if you're desperately awaiting a shipment of antibiotics or vaccines to deal with some outbreak, you don't have that integrated into the same platform; it's still atomized across multiple different data platforms. So data integration, data fusion, and then the application of AI and ML to summarize, explain and analyze that in ways that are much more powerful than what we currently have, I think is really useful for crisis response, including in a biological event.

items.question: How do you think AI investment should address the full process of turning a drug discovery into an available medical countermeasure?
items.object: AI-accelerated drug discovery and the wider countermeasure development process

If we could just have a DNA sequence or an RNA sequence and go, oh, that's what this does, based on some incredibly fancy AI techniques, that would be amazing. There's also creating better binding tools so that we can create things like nanobodies or incredibly good binding molecules that can inactivate viruses, so that we can rapidly create new countermeasures that are incredibly effective. All of that is extremely cool, and I think that we should be putting a lot of money into that kind of tool development. By the end of the day, you have something which looks like it will absolutely work. You've done whatever testing you can in silico. It binds perfectly. It doesn't seem to have any off-target binding. items.question: How do you think about the tradeoffs involved in following up on synthetic DNA orders flagged as sequences of concern?

Then you have the know your order check, and then you have the follow-up screening if it gets flagged. So if it's a sequence of concern, that's one of the sequences that's on the list, it raises a flag, and then the company would send an email and say, “Hey, we noticed that you were trying to order this sequence from Ebola. Why?” And then they would expect an email back that says, “Oh, we're working on an Ebola vaccine or an Ebola small molecule binder, and here's our grant code from our funder, and here's the biosafety officer's letter saying that they're aware of this project,” and you provide some documentation. And they go, “Okay, sure, that's fine.” And then they send it to you because that's completely legitimate. They obviously want to sell you that from a commercial perspective. They should sell you that because you're doing defensive research, and so that's absolutely fine.

But if they send an email and they say, “Hey, why are you ordering this?” and they're like, “No reason. Please just send it,” no, but we actually do need to understand why. And so you have this back and forth. Sometimes people are a bit cagey when they place an order for intellectual property reasons, or they don't want to get scooped. items.question: How do you view the movement toward making synthetic nucleic acid screening mandatory?
items.object: Moves toward mandatory screening of synthetic nucleic acid orders
items.answer:
I should say that currently screening is entirely voluntary in the UK. It's entirely voluntary in the US except for recipients of federal funds who, under a 2023 executive order, were mandated to purchase only from companies that screen. It's not entirely clear if that executive order still applies because it's been superseded by another executive order, but it seems as though most people are still continuing to comply with it just on the off chance that it does apply.

The European Biotech Act that the European Commission put out a draft version of last year also has a provision mandating screening, which is really encouraging. There's a bill in US Congress which has bipartisan support which mandates screening. There's a bill that's passed the California state legislature and a bill in the New York state legislature which is making its way through which also mandates screening. There's a clause in the Genetic Technology Act in New Zealand, clause 157, which also mandates screening. So there's a number of different moves towards making this mandatory, but currently as it stands, nowhere in the world actually has mandatory screening. items.question: How do you see the relationship between commercial incentives and security incentives for companies selling synthetic DNA?

items.answer: I think there is absolutely a misalignment between commercial incentives and security incentives. From a commercial perspective, you want it to be as frictionless as possible. items.question: How much confidence do you place in the International Gene Synthesis Consortium's voluntary screening commitments as a way to close the synthetic DNA security gap?
items.object: The International Gene Synthesis Consortium's voluntary screening commitments
items.answer:
In 2006 there was a Guardian article where an investigative reporter ordered, I think it was a 78 nucleotide or base pair segment of smallpox to his office, and you can't do anything with that. That's never going to be able to actually cause harm. But it was just illustrative: why was I, a journalist, able to purchase anything that has to do with smallpox and get it delivered to my offices? There's this whole security gap that's not being filled, and it really focused minds back in 2006.

In 2009, I believe it was, an organization called the IGSC was founded, which is the International Gene Synthesis Consortium. This is primarily companies that produce synthetic nucleic acids and which produce the screening tools, so it's really the key players involved in this industry. They basically voluntarily signed up to do screening despite there not being any sort of mandate at all back in 2009. Despite there not being pretty much any government pressure, they felt as an industry that if something were to happen from the products they sold, they didn't want to be held liable either in the court of public opinion or in the actual courts. So they said, we will come together, we will set standards for screening, and we will do screening. We want to do this proactively in the world.

I think this will have changed now because of the shifts and trends and patterns, but as of, I think, 2015, the claim was that 80% of synthetic nucleic acids sold in the world were sold by IGSC members who had voluntarily signed up to screen, which is really positive. But there have been red teaming exercises since by the Engineering Biology Research Consortium in the US, where they created fake profiles which were low legitimacy, medium legitimacy, and high legitimacy. High legitimacy being professor X at university Y, and low legitimacy being some guy at a residential address. They basically tried to create the max and min of institutional legitimacy and traditional factors of what you would look for.

They ordered from IGSC companies, and they told them ahead of time that they were going to be doing this red teaming exercise. They did it in coordination with the local FBI weapons of mass destruction coordinator, so this was all done in a very clean and above board way. They still found that three out of 20 companies that were IGSC members would sell to less legitimate profiles, even with sequences of concern, even above 200 base pairs, which is gene length.

items.question: How concerned are you that a centralized database for screening dangerous genetic sequences could itself create an information hazard?
items.object: The information hazard of centralized databases for screening potentially dangerous genetic sequences
items.answer: I had this question for a long time and I had the same concern for a long time and ultimately I had a conversation with someone who said well you know all of that information is already public domain. So we already know because it's not like we're talking about novel sequences, we're talking about existing sequences. It is not a difficult thing to find what the pathogens are that people have been concerned about historically. In fact, the voluntary guidance that the UK has produced, the Department of Science, Innovation, Technology has put out voluntary guidance for screening, links out to all of the pieces of legislation, the anti-terror crimes, ATCSA, the anti-terror crimes security I think act. SAPO which is the animal pathogens act. All of these things have schedules right they have annexes they have schedules and you can see what the organisms are that they're concerned about. This is all public knowledge and it's even linked out like I say by government documents to other government documents. So from there you can go what is the full genome of these organisms because again that's public information published on like PubMed or anything else and then you can get the full list of all of the genes that are of concern. I just don't think that that is that much of an infohazard because again it's all public information. I will say that many of the commercially available screening tools and there about six or seven have strong cryptographic encryption and it's not easy to brute force query them over and over again to try and find what is and isn't in scope of being flagged. items.question: How do you think about balancing public awareness of biosecurity threats against the risk of giving potential terrorists ideas?
items.object: The risk of raising malicious actors’ awareness through public biosecurity communication
items.answer:
It's an extremely difficult question that we run into all the time at the center for long-term resilience in our biocurity policy unit. It's just a perennial problem: how do you raise awareness with the right people without raising awareness with the wrong people? Obviously, we want to raise awareness with policy makers so that they know that this is a viable threat vector and then they address it. But we don't want to raise awareness with potential terrorists so that they go, “Wait, oh, this is a viable threat vector. Maybe I should use this.” It's really difficult.

There's a very good paper by Antonia Ulik. She just put it out. It is about how Boko Haram have used AI, and she has interviews with 57 ex-Boko Haram fighters in Nigeria. She went out to Nigeria, built relationships with these people over time and interviewed ex-Boko Haram fighters and asked them very clearly about their use of large language models in planning and carrying out terror activities. I recommend everyone read this paper. It is phenomenal. But what comes out top line is Boko Haram are actively using large language models, including jailbroken ones, to carry out and plan and increase the efficiency of their terror attacks.

So there is a real risk when we have these conversations that we raise the saliency and then malicious actors use the tools that are available to all of us to cause harm, right? And so it is an incredibly difficult thing to balance, and we are constantly reviewing and discussing what it is that we want to put out in the world and what it is we don't want to put out in the world, and what we want to put out into the world behind closed doors with a very targeted audience and what is appropriate to put out to a broader public. It's incredibly difficult.

items.question: How do you think about assigning responsibility and legal liability for an engineered pathogen release?
items.object: Responsibility and legal liability for an engineered pathogen release
items.answer:
I think that is the trillion dollar question right now because the tort and liability angle to all of this is not settled, and hopefully we will not have an incident, whether deliberate or accidental, involving engineered biological organisms. That would be bad and we don't want to see it in the world at all. But it may be that unless there is an incident that will never get settled because no one wants to take on the legal responsibility or liability ahead of time. No one should put their hand up and say, yes, okay, this will be my fault if it happens. But there's also a question of insurance, right? Like to what extent do you insure against this kind of thing and to what extent should we require insurance from AI companies or from synthesis companies or from whoever or from screening tool developers? How do you apportion liability in this?

I'm not a lawyer. I have absolutely no idea what the legal precedent and jurisprudence is here in various jurisdictions. I'm sure it'll differ, but there have been different arguments put before. So, again, I don't have a take on this, but I'll just, I guess, explain or put out some of the thinking that I've heard from others, which is if someone commits a mass casualty event with a weapon, like a Glock, the Glock company is not liable for the deaths that have occurred, right? If someone has sold that person a Glock and has not carried out the appropriate background checks, then that person, the gun salesperson, maybe is liable for some aspect of that. But ultimately the liability lies with the person that did the mass casualty event. And it's not the manufacturer of the bullets either that is liable.

So we have these frameworks that we can adapt from previous mass casualty events where we would say, well, it's not this person, it's not that person, but it's not clear that those things map necessarily one to one on an engineered pathogen release. And again then you get into the difference between deliberate versus accidental, right? If you have followed all procedures appropriately and you have all the appropriate paperwork and all the safeguards are in place and inspections are up to date, etc., but something goes wrong, like a valve fails and something gets vented out instead of in, sometimes things just happen. You can imagine a world in which everything has gone correctly but some sort of micro electronic circuit, like a chip, fails. Just happens, right? And then whose fault is it?

And so it just gets to be very difficult both in accidental and deliberate events. It's also not the case in deliberate events that we can necessarily even tell who it was, and I'm not going to get too deep into that, but the attribution piece is obviously—we have capabilities in that respect, but perhaps not the capabilities that we would like to see in the world. Perhaps they're not as mature as we'd like to see them or as widespread. Some jurisdictions will have much more mature capabilities in that respect than others. So, yeah, it gets to be pretty difficult.

items.question: Why do you see mandatory screening of synthetic biological sequences and their buyers as a useful legal intervention?
items.object: Mandatory screening of synthetic biological sequences and their buyers
items.answer: I think that that's where mandatory screening comes in as a really useful intervention, legal intervention, because it basically does what the gun salesperson check that this person's allowed to have a gun piece of legislation does. Effectively, it goes, should this person have ever been sold this? And if the answer is no, then you can start apportioning liability and blame, I guess, to the extent that that's useful. But if you don't have that, if it's all voluntary, if it's just like basically I can sell whatever I want to whoever I want, whenever I want—which is not exactly the case, to be fair. I should clarify that there is already legislation in place, like I mentioned the SAPO and ATCSA within the UK. So there's already that, and there's some implicit requirements to screen, but there's no explicit mandate to do so. items.question: Why do you regard organisms made entirely from molecules of the opposite chirality as a serious biological threat?
items.object: Mirror organisms and immune evasion
items.answer:
Mirror life is one that was new to me when it came up. I had never heard of it. I had during my PhD made mirror macromolecules, so I had made mirror peptides, but even while doing that no one had ever been like, oh what if you had a cell that was made up entirely of opposite chirality macromolecules, because that would have been a crazy idea. But then I realized that a lot of people were thinking about this and it wasn't such a crazy idea. In fact, it was a pretty real long-term threat. I think that's important to say. It's not going to happen tomorrow, but it is definitely on the horizon.

Your immune system, human immune systems, they recognize things in three dimensions and they're expecting things to be this shape. But instead they see the opposite shape, they can't bind it. The shape is wrong. We have no direct proof and we've not created a mirror organism. Thank god. So we can't test it out. But from first principles, it is very likely that immune activation would be much much lower and as a result we wouldn't be able to detect or clear that infection.

But then if you take it to the next level, it's not just human immune systems that rely on three-dimensional shapes and arrangements of atoms in space. It's actually animal immune systems. It's plant immune systems, which are very different, but they do have a form of immunity. Little amoebas in the sea, when they eat stuff, they're expecting it in order to digest it to be in a particular shape. Their enzymes act on things that are a particular shape.

And so you think, wow, if there were really a mirror organism and it breached containment or it were released deliberately into the world, there's no real way that we could actually stop it. We couldn't detect it because all of our diagnostics expect molecules to be in one particular shape and this would be in the other shape. Beyond not being able to detect it, how would we be able to treat it? We couldn't necessarily clear it as an infection in a person. It wouldn't have the same signs, wouldn't be able to produce virulence factors. So it wouldn't be able to attack your cells directly because all of its virulence factors would be the opposite shape.

items.question: Where would you draw the boundary for restrictions on mirror-life research?
items.object: Restrictions on research that directly creates self-replicating mirror organisms
items.answer:
If we don't fund research that leads directly to the creation of mirror life, if we prohibit research that leads directly to the creation of mirror life, then we avoid that end state where a self-replicating mirror organism exists and therefore we avoid all the consequences that might occur. You'll notice I'm choosing my words very carefully because there's a lot of debate about enabling technologies and things which lead us to that self-replicating organism that might be beneficial, mirror ribosomes, etc. And that's a separate conversation that I'm very happy to have. But ultimately, the end state of a self-replicating mirror organism is one which we should try to avoid to the greatest extent possible.

The German, I think it's called ZKBS, which is like the bureau for biocurity, has put out a statement on this being of concern. I took part in a round table with the government chief scientific adviser in the UK along with eight other experts, and we put out a report which is not an official government report but which basically says that this is something that we should be concerned about and that we should be careful with.

So this is something that people are taking seriously and there's a lot of people who are saying this is a bad thing. But there's nothing again in law that says that you can't do this.

items.question: What policies do you see as the highest-leverage ways to prevent research that leads directly to the creation of mirror life?

I'll talk about the ones that I know: UKRI, which is UK Research and Innovation that funds pretty much all publicly funded science in the UK; the National Science Foundation in the US; the European Research Council; and the welcome trust, because they have huge amounts of funding. I use those four as examples, but I would like for it to spread more widely, of course. That would already be a really big deal. That would be a first step. And again, when I say this research, I mean research that leads directly to the creation of mirror life.

items.question: What do you think the COVID pandemic revealed about the way we think about medical supply chains?
items.object: COVID-19 medical supply chains and overlooked manufacturing bottlenecks
items.answer: I think a lot of people realize that we don't make very much especially here in the UK. Different countries fared very differently. So the US and China obviously have much bigger domestic manufacturing bases than we do in the UK. Obviously the EU is somewhere in between because the EU is 27 countries. So it's not quite the same. And I think the realization that no matter how much money when you want something, you can't just have it if you don't make it because you have to wait for it to come from elsewhere and you have to bid for it because other people also want it. items.question: How do you assess the prospect of achieving domestic supply-chain sovereignty for medical preparedness?
items.object: Domestic supply-chain sovereignty and global interdependence in medical preparedness
items.answer: If you break it down, Ernston Young have a fantastic diagram from 2023 in a piece I think called the farmer supply chains of the future. They looked at a biobag. A biobag is a single-use plastic bag used for fermentation to produce biologic drugs and they took that one biobag and they were like, "How do we get this? How do you get to this bag?" Right? And there are five tiers of supply going from the petrol at the very bottom tier because it's a plastic bag so you need petrol to make the plastic all the way up to something like a much more complex sterilization equipment like you need a source of gamma radiation to sterilize the biobag so that you can then grow stuff in it that can produce that biologic drug. There are 95 components that go into making a single biobag and all of those are sourced from different countries. It is not the case that we live in a world where everything is like one big vertically integrated supply chain in one country that has total domestic sovereignty over what they make and we will never return to that. Maybe the closest we have to that is China, to some extent India, and to some extent the United States, but even then they don't actually have full domestic sovereignty in the United States and India in particular because of rare earth metals and minerals. And even if you have the rare earth metals, you mine them in your country. You're like, "Oh, I am sovereign. I have sovereign dominion and control over this resource." 95% of the purification and refining is in China. So you take it out of your soil and then you put it on a boat and it goes to China for the refining because you don't have a refinery for that rare earth metal in your own country no matter where you are because again 90 plus% of the refining happens in China and then they send it back to you. When it's not an accident, we see it in the straight of Hormuz. items.question: How do you think about whether regulatory specifications for drug packaging and vaccine vials can safely be relaxed?
items.object: Regulatory specifications for drug packaging and vaccine glass vials
items.answer:
If you market a drug, there's a lot of regulation around the packaging. The cardboard has to be a specific type of cardboard. The ink has to be a specific type of ink. The leaflet that goes inside has to be on a specific type of paper on which it has to be printed with another different specific type of ink. All of these things are specified. They're not random. It's not like whatever paper I happen to find and whatever cardboard and whatever ink that I'm going to source from wherever because it's cheaper or available or domestically manufactured. There are incredibly stringent specifications on this.

In some cases, yeah, I guess I'll say it. It seems pointless, right? I'm sure there are reasons. Regulation is usually written in blood. So if there is a specific ink and there is a specific paper and there's a specific cardboard, it's probably because at some point someone used the wrong ink or the wrong cardboard or the wrong paper and as a result the leaflet was unreadable. Someone couldn't read the side effects. They suffered side effects and that was bad. You can imagine that that's why that regulation exists. Usually regulation isn't just there to be annoying. There's probably something and I don't know the history of it. So I don't want to be overly cocky and say, “Oh, we should just do away with all this red tape.” There's probably a reason why it's there. It's worth questioning though what that reason is and then analyzing to what extent that could be flexed.

Some of it though is based on safety and efficacy stuff. The vaccine special glass for the glass vials in which the vaccine drug product is contained—that's because all the safety and efficacy testing and durability and longevity was done with the drug product in that glass. And you don't know if you use a different grade of glass, is it going to have the same UV filtration ability? So if you leave the vaccine doses out in the sun, are they going to degrade more quickly? Is a temperature change going to affect it more because it's a thinner type of glass or whatever it might be? I'm making it up at this point, but there are safety and efficacy reasons for some of this regulation, probably for most of the regulation. And so the question really becomes how much of it can you intelligently flex? How much of it can you offer options?

items.question: Why do you think flexibility in clinical-trial regulation during a health emergency needs to be planned in advance?
items.object: Advance planning for emergency clinical-trial flexibility and public trust
items.answer:
When we needed to have flexibility and regulation around clinical trials we did, but it's not great to do that ad hoc. It's not great to reactively go, oh no, something really bad has happened, now we need to make up a whole new system that we haven't tested or tried in the past in order to deal with this immediate threat that we're facing.

It needs to be much more proactive and thought about ahead of time, tested, stress tested. What are the preconditions that need to be met in order for phase one to be rolled into phase two, or whatever, 2A rolled into 2B? Have this set out ahead of time and planned and have a workflow or a framework or whatever you want to call it, to at least have thought about this ahead of time rather than doing it reactively and being like, oh no, terrible things are happening, let's do away with everything that we do usually.

Because that also doesn't help for trust reasons, right? People are expecting a drug to go through a specific process, and a lot of people had expressed antivax sentiment to me back in 2020, 2021 because they felt that the accelerated timeline for vaccines was suspicious and they thought, oh, this is the government colluding with big pharma. items.question: How do you assess medical stockpiling as a response to fragile supply chains?
items.object: Medical stockpiling as a response to fragile supply chains
items.answer:
I'm a big fan of stockpiling. Some people hate it, some people really like it. I'm in the latter camp. I think stockpiling is very useful. I think, however, that we need to recognize the limits of stockpiling. One example that I think is good is the strategic active pharmaceutical ingredient reserve, modeled on the strategic petroleum reserve. It's two physical locations in the United States which are supposed to be filled up with active pharmaceutical ingredient. So it's not the end thing that's going to go into people's arms or into people's mouths, but the things that you need to mix together basically in order to make the final drug. And that's, I think, a really good idea.

I will say that the execution seemingly is lacking. A US general closely involved in setting it up said, I think two years after it was created, that it was supposed to be 25% full by that point, but it was 2% full. So declaring that you're going to stockpile is one thing. Having a legal framework or a legal mandate is one thing. You then actually have to do it.

Then we get into an issue which is manifold but primarily twofold. One, it costs money, and it costs money now for a thing that might happen in the future. That is the type of spend-to-save thinking which has been very difficult to sell in a constrained macroeconomic environment, as I know very clearly from having had conversations with policy makers and tried to convince them that it's worth spending to save in the future. Very difficult when government finances are otherwise constrained.

The other thing is that if everyone decides to stockpile at the same time, and they all decide to stockpile the same stuff because pretty much we all need the same sort of critical medicines list, then prices skyrocket. It's just what they were making before, but now instead of one or two governments wanting it, 198 or 193, whatever, want that same thing in order to stockpile. So there's a real difficulty there.

There's also not necessarily a need to have it at a national level, especially in institutions like the European Union where you can have centralized stockpiling. When I say centralized, I mean centralized relative to each country, decentralized relative to each other: several different nodes where there are stockpiles that have each thing, and then they can go out from nodes to countries. It's all one big contiguous land mass, which really helps. We don't have that in the UK, which is a big problem.

items.question: Why do you see stock rotation as a difficult part of maintaining medical reserves?
items.object: Stock rotation and the sustainable operation of medical reserves
items.answer:
You have these stockpiles. They're full of stuff. They're coming to the end of their life. What do you do? You just burn it? Because that looks terrible. No one wants to then replenish your stockpile. If it was like, oh, we spent all this money five years ago to be ready, didn't use it—good, right? It's great we didn't use it because there was no big biological event. But now we're just going to burn it and we're going to spend all that money again. The public is not going to look kindly on that kind of expenditure.

So what needs to happen is, to the extent that it's possible, the stock needs to be rotated back into the healthcare system so that it's used and it's replenished on an ongoing basis. And that's much more difficult to do with active pharmaceutical ingredients, because you basically need to buy the active pharmaceutical ingredients at one point, store them for a while, then sell them back to the people that sold them to you so that they can put it back into their supply chain and sell them to people down the line who are going to make it into drug products, etc. And it's just quite messy and difficult. But you don't want to store drug products because those are really specific. Active pharmaceutical ingredients give you more flexibility, right?

So the whole thing is just quite difficult, and governments, I think, feel very constrained from the optics side of things: how do we explain to people that we're spending to save in the future? How do we explain to people that this is part of national security? How do we do stock rotation effectively?

In the UK at least we have the NHS. So if it is drug products or PPE, and if it's the same type of PPE that's being used in the NHS, you can cycle into the NHS. So that's good. Not every country has a public healthcare system in that way, and therefore it makes it more difficult. Thinking globally rather than just UK, EU, US, stock rotation then involves the government selling to private healthcare systems. What if they make a loss? Does it look like they're subsidizing the private sector? Maybe they won't get what they paid for because the private healthcare system is like, well, I'll just buy it from the source, why would I buy it from you? So it can be very difficult to do this in a way that doesn't look like corruption.

I think it's great that there's some public thinking. I would encourage all governments, including the UK government, to publish a stockpiling strategy that is available for third party scrutiny.

items.question: Why do you think medical stockpiling remains vulnerable to spending cuts even when it costs little relative to the total government budget?
items.object: The political vulnerability of spending on medical stockpiles and domestic vaccine manufacturing
items.answer:
Yeah, usually it's not very expensive, but the problem is that things can be not very expensive compared to the total government budget and yet still be politically expedient. I'll give you an example. In the last few years of the Rishi Sunak government here in the UK, there was a budget shortfall and they were trying to plug a hole. I think it was something like a £5 billion hole. £5 billion is 0.5%. A trillion, right, that's the government budget: pensions and healthcare and everything, defence, etc. So they were looking for £5 billion, which is a lot of money but ultimately not a lot of money.

So what did they decide to do? Well, there was this thing called the V-Mic, the Vaccine Manufacturing Innovation Center, and it was created by Theresa May's government in the wake of the Sierra Leone, West Africa Ebola crisis in 2016. So in 2017, 2018, they stood up this thing. It was supposed to be a sovereign domestic vaccine manufacturing capability for the UK. Money was put in by the UK taxpayer through the government, by the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, by Oxford University, by Cambridge University, I believe maybe by Imperial College London. So university partners, government, they built this thing together.

I think they broke ground in like 2018, and it had partial operational capacity during COVID. Some doses were manufactured at V-Mic, as far as I know, because it provided some cycles in the system, which is exactly what it's supposed to do, but it wasn't a fully complete facility. The facility was completed in 2022, at which point the government needed to find some money for this budget shortfall, so they sold it for £200 million. £200 million, so 0.2 billion, when they were looking for five out of a budget of a thousand. So Catalent, a United States company, now owns the UK's sovereign vaccine manufacturing center. We don't have one anymore in the UK.

So sometimes it's just about a couple hundred million here, a couple hundred million there. So yes, it's not very expensive to stockpile, but if it's a couple hundred million, it's the kind of thing that will very quickly get done away with in order to look politically fiscally responsible, prudent.

items.question: How do you think governments should balance sovereign manufacturing of critical supplies with reliance on other countries?
items.object: Sovereign manufacturing of critical materials and medical countermeasures
items.answer:
It is not desirable to fully reshore everything and have an entirely concentrated supply chain all in country and then go, “I rely on no one externally,” because that is just as fragile as owning nothing. If someone undermines one component within your country and you don't have existing links out to other countries, then suddenly you are in just as difficult a position as you would be if you don't control anything. So there is, we say in French, a correct middle, a middle path. And that looks something like partial reshoring and massive friend shoring.

There are some things that we should do in country. And the UK government clearly agrees. I know I'm using a lot of UK government positions, but that's where I work. As of this morning, the UK government has fully nationalized British Steel. They had already taken control of the facility and were subsidizing its operation to the tune of 1.3 million pounds a day to ensure that there was still steel being made in Britain for Britain. They make the type of steel that's required for warships, so it has knock-on effects on defense manufacturing to control or not control this source of steel. A big deal, right? But they did it because it was important.

That same thinking is unfortunately not yet applied to medical countermeasures. And we've been trying to shift that over time. It's quite difficult, but there is kind of a zeitgeist at the minute that we can tap into with the whole NATO commitment, 5%, 3.5 plus 1.5, for national security and defense. We have been trying to make the argument that since biological security is national security, it would make sense for the government, as part of its 5% commitment, maybe in the 1.5% which is for national security rather than defense, to make investments and co-investments with private industry to reshore some aspects of medical countermeasure manufacturing.

items.question: Why do you see feeder industries as a major obstacle to bringing antibiotic manufacturing back to the UK?
items.object: Feeder industries as a constraint on reshoring antibiotic manufacturing
items.answer:
One of the issues with reshoring is feeder industry. I said this when I was giving evidence in the House of Lords for an inquiry on medicine security, and this comes from someone who worked at FISA for 37 years who oversaw the offshoring initially to China and to India. At the time, that was what was deemed economically efficient without a national security lens applied to it, because it was the late '90s and things were going well, fall of the Berlin Wall, and global capitalism was prospering. So offshoring as a sort of economically efficient model was the thing that everyone was doing. He oversaw some of that, and he was talking about how that eroded domestic manufacturing capacity.

The problem is that these are living organisms that need to ferment and produce this antibiotic. In order to do that they need aqueous ammonia, and aqueous ammonia is produced industrially mostly as fertilizer. But the UK has moved away from aqueous ammonia as fertilizer towards other forms of fertilizer. So the aqueous ammonia plants used to have two customers: the places that were fermenting antibiotics and the places that needed fertilizer. Both of those were offshored or closed down. So the aqueous ammonia plant closed down.

So you bring back a factory, you're like, “I'm going to put a billion pounds towards getting a new factory” for these fermentation products, like other antibiotics. Great. Where are you going to get the aqueous ammonia? You're not going to make it domestically because it doesn't have another industry. It would just feed that one plant. So you're still going to have a foreign choke point in your manufacturing process because you don't make the aqueous ammonia anymore. All the feeder industries that used to exist have now also closed down. So it's not as easy as just, “We're going to reshore this or that.” You have to think intelligently about coordinated international industrial strategy.

items.question: How would you like allied countries to coordinate medical countermeasure manufacturing through friend shoring?
items.object: Friend shoring of medical countermeasure manufacturing
items.answer:
Austria has put €150 million—I say just, it was about a year and a half ago—of taxpayer money into building a third generation cephalosporin factory, fully integrated with, I believe it was Sandos, which is great. Let's not also build a third generation cephalosporin factory in the UK in partnership with Sandos, because if we need those, we can have advantageous agreements with Austria as an allied and partner nation and say, “Hey, we actually make something different. We will give you that at a preferential rate if you give us this at a preferential rate.”

France has just put a stack of money, I think about 10 million, but that's just a small part of it, into a new paracetamol factory in the southwest of France. So let's not put 10 million pounds into building a new paracetamol factory in the UK, because we can just get that from our French allies across the channel at a preferential rate.

So let's look at what other countries are doing in a really rational way. And I say “let's” for the UK, but every country should look at what other countries in their vicinity, and who are their allies and partners, are doing. Make a decision as to what they think is a priority, coordinate at an industrial level on the industrial strategy that they are going to adopt, and see how they can fill the gaps that each other has in an intelligent and coordinated way. You purchase from people who have reshored another portion of what you haven't, at preferential rates amongst allies and partners.

Allies and partners are going to largely be geographically collocated, the EU, et cetera. But they can also be other middle powers. It can be Canada, it can be Australia, it can be South Korea, allies and partners. Obviously, the closer the geography, the easier it is to then move trucks in a biological event where things are closed down and locked down, right? So there is a geographical advantage to doing that friend shoring with people nearby, but not exclusively.

To me, that's a really big solution, but it requires a big effort because it requires international collaboration. It requires people to want to work together internationally to achieve a mutual aim and a mutually beneficial goal, and that's not always that easy.

items.question: How do you assess the value and environmental tradeoffs of the UK's focus on pharmaceutical fill and finish?
items.object: The UK's pharmaceutical fill-and-finish industry
items.answer: The UK is very depleted on API manufacturing and does a lot of fill and finish. So they get stuff that's basically ready and they fill the vials with the stuff that they've received and they finish. So they put the label on it, put it in a box that meets the criteria and then ship it back out. That fill and finish is quite a high value step because it has to be done appropriately in order to be marketable, has to be done with specific materials and according to specific good manufacturing practices. And it's much less environmentally intensive. You don't have the sort of small molecule pollution that comes from making APIs, which is one of the reasons why we offshored that, by the way, is because we were quite happy for India and China to produce all of this for the rest of the world and pollute their rivers rather than ours, both from a carbon emission perspective but also from a small molecule pollution perspective.

items.question: Why do you regard the concentration of active pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturing in China and India as a supply-chain choke point?
items.object: Concentration of active pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturing in China and India
items.answer: I think we should always remember that there's now a really high degree of concentration in API manufacturing in China and India, even relative to the EU and US, because of this offshore program that several governments oversaw and private industry drove. It didn't happen by accident. In the same way that ASML is kind of the natural choke point for AI, Chinese and Indian factories are the natural choke point for active pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturing. We've seen this actually in the report that I mentioned earlier, boosting supply chain resilience. You highlight two vignettes. One was production in Venezuela, and the facility just had tons of issues. It was just kind of an old facility and it regularly had issues, and as a result there was a shortage for 1,780 days, if I recall correctly, throughout Europe because the facility just wasn't producing what it needed to produce. And there was an explosion at a facility, I believe this was in China, that just led to a total lack of production of some antibiotics that just didn't reach the UK for a while. NHS England did a benchmarking survey where they tried to understand where an antibiotic was coming from. They're like, okay, we have seven dosage forms we can give to patients, where do they all come from? They realized they actually had two suppliers in the seven dosage forms. And basically the question becomes, well, what happens if a typhoon blows through that city and damages power cables and the factories go offline? Suddenly there's no antibiotic reaching patients in the UK after whatever time it takes to exhaust the stocks that already exist in the UK. How does that affect UK patients or European patients or US patients very far away from where that's made? So yeah, there are similar choke points definitely.
